title: Job 6:21–30
context: Job presses his charge against the friends. They have become nothing to him; they see a terror and are afraid (6:21). He has asked them for no gift, ransom, or rescue (6:22–23), only for honest instruction: “Teach me, and I will hold my peace. Cause me to understand my error” (6:24). Upright words have force, but their reproof proves nothing, and they treat the words of a desperate man as wind (6:25–26). In sharp language he accuses them of treating the vulnerable as merchandise (6:27), then pleads with them to look at him, to turn back, and to see that his cause is righteous and his tongue free of injustice (6:28–30). Both traditions read Job’s words as honest lament and protest, without endorsing every charge or condemning him for making them, and leave the book’s later verdict on the friends (42:7) to do its own work.

verses.text: For now you are nothing. You see a terror, and are afraid.
verses.arminianNotes: “For now you are nothing. You see a terror, and are afraid.” Arminian readers note Job’s insight that his friends are frightened by his suffering. Fear may be shaping their counsel, making them quick to explain rather than slow to sympathize.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job naming the friends’ fear in the face of calamity. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s perception of his friends, and both see in it a caution for any comforter tempted to defend themselves against another’s pain.

verses.text: Did I ever say, ‘Give to me’? or, ‘Offer a present for me from your substance’?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether he ever said, “Give to me,” or asked them to offer a gift from their wealth. Arminian readers note that Job had asked for nothing costly. His request was only for loyalty and understanding, which makes their failure harder to bear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the modesty of what Job sought. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s defense that he made no unreasonable demands, and both see in it the point that compassion often costs little but means much.

verses.text: or, ‘Deliver me from the adversary’s hand’? or, ‘Redeem me from the hand of the oppressors’?
verses.arminianNotes: Nor did he ask them to deliver him from the adversary or redeem him from oppressors. Arminian readers note that Job did not ask them to rescue him by force or ransom. He only wanted them to stand with him in his suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job emphasizing that he asked nothing beyond friendship. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing Job’s point that the friends had only to offer sympathy, and both see in it the value of presence over solutions.

verses.text: “Teach me, and I will hold my peace. Cause me to understand my error.
verses.arminianNotes: “Teach me, and I will hold my peace. Cause me to understand my error.” Arminian readers note Job’s openness to correction, if it is true and specific. He is willing to be taught, but he wants real instruction rather than general accusation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a sincere request for understanding. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that Job is not closed to truth, and both affirm that honest instruction must address the actual situation rather than assume guilt.

verses.text: How forcible are words of uprightness! But your reproof, what does it reprove?
verses.arminianNotes: “How forcible are words of uprightness! But your reproof, what does it reprove?” Arminian readers note that Job values honest words, but finds the friends’ rebuke empty because it does not fit his case. Truth must be rightly applied.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job distinguishing true words from misapplied ones. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a challenge to the friends’ reasoning and as a reminder that correct principles can be wrongly applied to a particular sufferer.

verses.text: Do you intend to reprove words, since the speeches of one who is desperate are as wind?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether they mean to reprove his words, when the speeches of a desperate man are like wind. Arminian readers note his plea that words spoken in despair be heard with understanding. A sufferer’s cries should not be judged as formal arguments.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a call for compassion in weighing the words of the desperate. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as asking comforters to listen to the person behind the words, and both affirm that lament should be heard with patience.

verses.text: Yes, you would even cast lots for the fatherless, and make merchandise of your friend.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says they would cast lots for the fatherless and make merchandise of their friend. Arminian readers read this as sharp rhetoric from a wounded man. They report his charge honestly without treating it as a measured verdict on the friends.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear an angry accusation and decline to take it as a balanced judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, as part of Job’s protest, and leave the final assessment of the friends to the book’s own verdict (42:7).

verses.text: Now therefore be pleased to look at me, for surely I will not lie to your face.
verses.arminianNotes: “Now therefore be pleased to look at me, for surely I will not lie to your face.” Arminian readers hear Job inviting his friends to see him truly. He appeals to his honesty and asks them to judge by what they see, not by what they assume.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a plea for honest attention and a claim to integrity. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job asking to be met as a person, and both see in it a model of the openness that comfort requires.

verses.text: Please return. Let there be no injustice. Yes, return again. My cause is righteous.
verses.arminianNotes: “Please return. Let there be no injustice… My cause is righteous.” Arminian readers note Job’s plea for his friends to reconsider. He maintains his integrity and asks them not to wrong him by assuming guilt where there is none.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear Job’s insistence on his integrity, which the prologue affirms (1:1; 2:3). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job defending his cause before his friends, without treating his claim as a denial of all human sinfulness.

verses.text: Is there injustice on my tongue? Can’t my taste discern mischievous things?
verses.arminianNotes: “Is there injustice on my tongue? Can’t my taste discern mischievous things?” Arminian readers note Job’s confidence that he can tell right from wrong. He believes his words, though rash, are not unjust, and he asks his friends to recognize this.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear Job’s claim to moral discernment, held in tension with his later confession that he spoke of what he did not understand (42:3). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as closing Job’s reply with a plea for fair hearing, and both let the rest of the book weigh his words.
